lire.p1: Each of you answered on your own, without seeing the other's answers. This report puts your two sets of answers side by side, topic by topic, to show you where you agree and where you don't see things the same way.
lire.p2: The questions are based on research in couple psychology: studies that followed couples for years, and the questionnaires marriage counsellors use before a wedding. This report isn't a diagnosis. It's a starting point for talking, with the right topics in the right order.
lire.p3: The easiest way is for each of you to read it on your own, then talk it through together, one topic at a time. If you're not sure where to start, go straight to your next four conversations.
lire.nn: One of you marked this topic as non-negotiable.
lire.poids: A question that shapes a whole life (a child, where to live, fidelity, the money you share) weighs three times as much as an everyday one in your scores. It carries this label.

synthese.intro: Two numbers sum up your assessment. The first shows how much you want the same life together. The second shows how each of you feels in the relationship right now. The two don't always go together: you can be very aligned and going through a rough patch, or the other way round.
synthese.alignementAide: How closely your answers about life together match. Decisive topics count triple.
synthese.climatAide: How each of you feels in the relationship right now.
synthese.radarAide: The closer the shape gets to the edge, the more your answers meet in that area. The exact figures are in the next chapter.
synthese.rassembleIntro: The big questions where you answered exactly the same.

onde.texte: You want roughly the same life, and you see it the same way. You do have gaps, but only a few: it's a good time to talk about them while they're still small.

proches.texte: You agree on the essentials, with a few topics where you don't see things the same way. That's the case for most couples who are doing well.

creuser.titre: Close, with a few topics to explore
creuser.texte: You agree on a lot of things, but several topics set you apart. Nothing alarming as long as you talk about them, and that's exactly what this assessment is for.

apprivoiser.texte: You have fairly different ways of seeing life together. It says nothing about your love, but it does mean some topics need real conversations, and compromises.

visions.texte: On many topics, you don't want the same thing. Some couples live very well with that, others don't: the most important thing is to know which of these gaps really matter to each of you.

beau.texte: You both feel good in your relationship.

nuages.texte: Things are going well, with a few points where one of you feels less good.

variable.texte: There's good, and some harder patches at the moment.

orageux.texte: One of you, or both, isn't feeling very good in the relationship right now.

tempete.texte: Things aren't going well at the moment. This assessment can help put words to it, and a couples counsellor can help you go further.

carte.intro: Each bar shows how closely your answers match in one area, from 0 to 100%. How your relationship feels right now isn't about agreeing, so it has its own part.

conversations.intro: The topics where your answers are furthest apart, on what matters most, one per area. Keep one per evening, when things are calm, rather than all at once.
conversations.aucune: You don't have any gap to work on: your answers are close or identical everywhere. That's rare! Make the most of it and talk about what brings you together.

bloquants.intro: Gaps on questions that one of you marked "non-negotiable". These are the first topics to raise, without trying to convince the other that evening: understand first.
bloquants.aucun: No sticking points: none of your gaps is on a topic one of you marked as non-negotiable.
bloquants.nnTitre: What's non-negotiable for each of you
bloquants.nnIntro: The topics where each of you said you couldn't compromise, with their answer.

ombre.intro: On the topics that matter most, you said what {{nom}} would answer. When you didn't know, you said so: this chapter gathers those topics. They aren't problems, they're questions to ask.

peu.texte: On only {{n}} topics, you didn't know what {{nom}} would answer. You know their way of seeing things well.

quelques.texte: On {{n}} topics, you didn't know what {{nom}} would answer. That's the case for most couples: people rarely talk about everything.

large.titre: A large share of blind spots
large.texte: On {{n}} topics, you didn't know what {{nom}} would answer. That isn't bad news: it's the list of conversations you haven't had yet.

ombre.listeTitre: The topics you don't know about
ombre.listeAide: Each one is a question to ask {{nom}}, as it is. Decisive topics carry their label.
ombre.aucune: You were able to answer for {{nom}} every time. So the report compares your answers with what you imagine theirs to be: the next step is to check with {{nom}}.

climat.intro: These questions aren't looking for agreement: they show how each of you is experiencing the relationship right now. A gap here means you're not living the same relationship, which happens much more often than people think.
climat.parDomaineAide: For the areas with questions about how you feel (arguments, intimacy and the general mood), each of you on the same line, from 0 to 100%. Two markers far apart: you aren't living the same thing.
climat.ecart: You don't feel it the same way
climat.sens: On each line, the left end is where things are going best, and the right end where they're going least well.

signaux.intro: Researchers who have been watching couples for decades have spotted a few ways of arguing that, once they become a habit, wear a relationship down far more than the arguments themselves. Everyone does them sometimes. What matters is how often, and what you do afterwards.
signaux.fin: If one of these comes up often for you, it's not a life sentence: it's exactly what a couples counsellor helps you change, and it can be changed.

roles.intro: For each topic, the line goes from "mostly {{a}}" to "mostly {{b}}". The two markers show what each of you answered.
roles.chacunPlusTexte: It's very common: you see what you do better than what the other does. The best thing is to list together what each of you takes care of, without keeping score.
roles.desequilibre: You agree: it's mostly {{nom}}. Is that OK for both of you?
roles.accord: You see it the same way.
roles.aucun: There's no question of this kind in your assessment.

fin.feuilleIntro: One topic a week, in this order. Tick them off as you go.
fin.ombreEtape: Ask {{nom}} the {{n}} questions from your blind spots
fin.refaireTexte: To see what has moved, and what has stayed put.

suite.p1: A report doesn't change anything on its own: what counts are the conversations it starts. Here's how to go about it, based on what works for couples who talk well.
conseils: One topic per evening, no more. Start with the easiest one to get into the rhythm.
Pick a calm moment, with no phones, and not in the middle of an argument.
Talk about what you feel ("I'm afraid that...") rather than about what the other person does.
The point of the first chat is to understand the other person, not to convince them. A decision can wait until the following week.
If things heat up, take a twenty-minute break and come back to it later. It works better than you'd think.
suite.refaire: Doing the assessment again in six months or a year shows what has changed between you. Lots of couples redo it at every big step: moving in together, getting married, having a baby.
suite.aide: This assessment is a tool for talking, not a diagnosis. If you're going through a difficult time, a couples counsellor or therapist can help you go further.
suite.violence: If you're afraid of your partner, this assessment isn't made for your situation. In the UK, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline (0808 2000 247) answers for free, 24/7, and in the US the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233).

This report puts the two side by side on those topics: where you're sure you think alike, where you know you don't see things the same way, and where you don't know. Your other answers are listed in each area.
lire.p3: Read it for yourself first. Then, if {{b}} is willing to talk about it, the four conversations and your blind spots show where to start. And if one day {{b}} wants to answer too, an assessment done together will replace your guesses with their answers.

suite.p1: A report doesn't change anything on its own: what counts is what you do with it. You did it alone, and that's already a way of seeing clearly. Here's how to go about what comes next.
conseils: Start by rereading your blind spots: they're simple questions to ask {{nom}}, without mentioning the report if you'd rather not.
Check your guesses one by one, starting with the conversations in the report: "I thought you'd say... is that right?"
Pick a calm moment, with no phones, and not in the middle of a tense one.
Talk about what you feel ("I'm afraid that...") rather than about what the other does.
If {{nom}} doesn't want to talk about it for now, this report still serves you: it says what matters to you, and what doesn't sit right. A relationship counsellor can also see you on your own.
suite.refaire: Doing the assessment together, when {{nom}} is willing, will replace your guesses with their answers. Lots of couples do it at every big step: moving in together, getting married, having a baby.

paragraphes: A relationship assessment, sometimes called a couples check-up, is a moment you take to look at where your relationship stands, to see what's going well and what isn't. You can do it with a couples counsellor, in a session, or on your own with a list of questions.

Quiz Couple's relationship assessment is done online, each of you on your own phone. You answer 100 concrete questions about twelve parts of life as a couple (money, everyday life, children, intimacy, arguments, etc.), without seeing the other's answers. For example: "Your money as a couple, ideally...", with four answers, from "All shared" to "Separate money, case by case". If you both give the same answer, that's an agreement. If your answers are far apart, that's a gap, and the gaps are what's worth talking about.

Once you've both answered, the full assessment costs {{prix}} for the two of you. It opens on the page straight away, and you get your assessment as a PDF by email, to keep. Your answers sit side by side, question by question, with questions to help you talk about each gap.

A lot of couples only talk about some subjects when things go wrong: money after a big purchase, children the day the question comes up, or splitting the chores in the middle of an argument... Assessing your relationship is a way to talk about them before, with a clear head.

The assessment also shows you what you don't know about each other. There are the subjects where you agree without ever having said so, and the ones where each of you thought the other saw things the same way. Those are often the ones that end in arguments, so it's worth finding them while things are calm.

utilite.solo: And if your partner doesn't feel like it, you can do it on your own: you answer for yourself and, on the topics that matter most, you say what you think your partner would answer.

items.a: Allow about 20 minutes each. Every answer is saved: you can take a break and pick up later.

items.q: Will my partner see my answers?
items.a: Yes, once you've both finished: the report puts your answers side by side, that's the whole point. Before that, nobody sees anything.

items.q: Why do you have to pay to see the result?
items.a: Because the result is the report: your answers compared topic by topic, with ways to talk about them. The questions are free, and you only pay at the end, if you want the report.

items.q: If I do it on my own, will my partner be told?
items.a: No. Nothing is sent to them, and only you see the report. You answer for yourself and, on the topics that matter most, in their place, or "I don't know".

items.q: What if we don't live together, or don't have children?
items.a: It works too. Six questions about your situation, asked along the way, adapt what follows: a couple who don't live together yet answer about what they imagine, for example.
No. The questions draw on research in couple psychology, but the assessment is a tool to know what to talk about, not a diagnosis. The report can also be a starting point with a professional.

items.q: What if we don't like the report?
items.a: It's made from your answers, and it may say something other than what you hoped. Once provided, it isn't refunded: before paying, you ask to receive it right away. As long as it hasn't been provided, you can withdraw. And if there's a problem with the file, we sort it out.
They're used only for your assessment and never sold. They're erased 60 days after the last answer without payment, six months after payment otherwise, and either of you can delete everything before.

final.texte: 20 minutes each, and you'll know what you agree on and what you need to talk about.

lp.avertissement: Together, this assessment shows each of you the other's answers. If you're afraid of your partner, do it on your own, or not at all: a domestic abuse helpline can talk with you, free and anonymously.
